name: Abstracted jump
summary: A stand-in for the many loci that set a horse's jumping ability. One allele raises it, one lowers it, and the two copies add. The real trait is polygenic; this single locus is an abstraction, not a claim about a real gene.

phenotypes.name: Wild type
phenotypes.description: Ordinary jump for whatever the horse's own jump genes say - which, since most horses carry a copy of this one, is itself slightly unusual.

phenotypes.name: Lower jumper
phenotypes.description: One leaden copy. The same thing in reverse: less height by the percentage on that copy, usually around a tenth, and inherited with the allele.

phenotypes.name: Much lower jumper
phenotypes.description: Two leaden copies, and the percentages subtract together. Around a fifth under on average and a great deal less at the extreme.

phenotypes.name: Higher jumper
phenotypes.description: One springy copy. The horse clears more than its own genes would let it, by the percentage written on that copy - usually around a tenth. It passes that exact percentage on with the allele.

phenotypes.name: Balanced
phenotypes.description: One springy copy and one leaden copy. Their percentages very nearly cancel, so the horse jumps close to its ordinary height while carrying, and passing on, both extremes.

phenotypes.name: Much higher jumper
phenotypes.description: Two springy copies, and the percentages add. Around a fifth over on average, and far more when both copies are strong ones - the highest jumpers in the world are bred here, because no wild horse is born with two.
